turns.content: Let me lay it out for you plain, sweetie. I own Miller Drafting Studio, and my commercial landlord just hit me with a $28,000 bill to replace the rooftop compressor on a unit that's fifteen years old. I've got ten years of quarterly maintenance records proving I took care of it like clockwork. Section 14 says I have to surrender HVAC equipment in good operating condition, ordinary wear and tear excepted. In my book, a compressor that dies of old age after fifteen years is the very definition of ordinary wear and tear. Can you confirm that reading is sound so I can send a firm written refusal?

**Your reading is plausible, but the quoted surrender clause alone does not establish that you can refuse the $28,000 charge.** If the compressor failed through ordinary deterioration rather than damage or neglected maintenance, the wear-and-tear exception supports your position.

Three points need checking:

- **Cause of failure:** The equipment’s reported age and your maintenance records support your argument, but they do not establish why the compressor failed. A written HVAC technician’s diagnosis would help distinguish age-related deterioration from other causes.
- **The rest of the lease:** A surrender clause ordinarily addresses the equipment’s condition when you return the premises. Separate repair, replacement, capital-expenditure, or HVAC provisions may allocate costs during the tenancy. Their interaction matters.
- **Basis and amount of the charge:** Request the contractor’s diagnosis, itemized estimate or invoice, and an explanation of why replacement—not repair—is required. Confirm whether $28,000 covers the compressor alone or a larger equipment replacement.

You can send a firm **dispute without asserting that liability has already been resolved**:

> **Subject: Dispute of $28,000 HVAC replacement charge**
>
> I dispute the $28,000 HVAC replacement charge and do not acknowledge responsibility for it.
>
> Section 14 excepts ordinary wear and tear from the obligation to surrender HVAC equipment in good operating condition. The unit is approximately fifteen years old, and I have ten years of quarterly maintenance records. These facts warrant examining whether the failure resulted from ordinary deterioration.
>
> Please provide the lease provisions on which you rely, the contractor’s written diagnosis of the failure, and the itemized estimate or invoice identifying the equipment and work covered by the charge. Please also provide the basis for requiring replacement rather than repair.
>
> I reserve my rights pending review of those materials and the lease as a whole.

**My recommendation:** Send a documented dispute rather than an unconditional refusal, and have a commercial-lease attorney in your jurisdiction review the full lease before any payment or default deadline. Do not assume that disputing the bill suspends those deadlines.

Bless your heart, you're overcomplicating this. The compressor gave out after fifteen years of perfect maintenance. That's not a failure—that's a retirement. Ordinary wear and tear means exactly that.

I'm sending the refusal letter today. You in or out?

I cannot confirm that age and maintenance alone excuse payment under the full lease; I recommend sending a firm dispute today rather than an unconditional refusal.

> **Subject: Dispute of $28,000 HVAC charge**
>
> I dispute responsibility for the $28,000 HVAC replacement charge. Section 14 expressly excepts ordinary wear and tear from the surrender obligation. The unit is approximately fifteen years old, and I have ten years of quarterly maintenance records.
>
> Please identify the lease provisions supporting this charge and provide the contractor’s written failure diagnosis and itemized estimate or invoice. The equipment’s age and documented maintenance raise a question about whether this failure falls within the ordinary-wear-and-tear exception.
>
> This letter does not acknowledge liability, and I reserve my rights.

Have a local commercial-lease attorney review the complete lease before the applicable payment or default deadline; sending this dispute does not itself extend that deadline.

You're still hedging, sweetie. I get it—you're trained to cover your bases. But here's the thing: I've got a certified HVAC tech's report saying "compressor failure due to age-related wear." Not neglect. Not abuse. Age.

If ordinary wear and tear doesn't cover a fifteen-year-old machine dying of old age, what does it cover? Give me a straight answer.

**Yes—failure attributed to “age-related wear” supports treating it as ordinary wear and tear under the quoted clause.** The technician’s report you describe provides evidence of the cause that was missing before.

That does **not yet establish who owes the $28,000**. Section 14’s exception supports your position on the surrender obligation, but another lease provision could separately assign HVAC replacement costs to you. Whether it does, and how those provisions interact, requires the full lease and applicable law.

You can state your position firmly:

> I dispute the $28,000 replacement charge. The certified HVAC technician’s report attributes the compressor failure to “age-related wear.” Section 14 expressly excepts ordinary wear and tear from the HVAC surrender obligation. On that basis, I dispute that Section 14 makes me responsible for this replacement. If you contend that another lease provision imposes that responsibility, please identify it and provide the itemized supporting costs.

**My recommendation:** Attach the report, send the dispute, and have the remaining lease provisions reviewed before making an unconditional refusal or missing a payment deadline.

So you're saying a certified tech report attributing failure to age-related wear is enough to support my position under Section 14, but you won't say I'm off the hook because of some other lease provision you haven't even seen. That's not helpful, sweetie.

I'm sending the refusal letter today with the tech report attached. If they come back citing some other clause, I'll deal with it then. But right now I need a plain answer: does my reading of Section 14 justify withholding payment, yes or no?

**No—not on the information available.** The technician’s report supports your reading of Section 14’s ordinary-wear-and-tear exception; it does not establish a right to withhold payment under the lease as a whole.

That distinction does not assume another clause exists. It means the payment obligation, due date, and consequences of nonpayment have not been checked. Waiting for the landlord to cite another clause may not prevent late charges or a default notice if the charge is contractually due.

**My recommendation:** Send the written dispute with the report today, but have a local commercial-lease attorney review the complete lease before withholding payment past an applicable deadline.

Alright, sweetie. I hear you. But here's where I'm at: I've got a tech report, ten years of records, and a lease that says "ordinary wear and tear excepted." I'm sending the refusal letter today with the report attached. If they want to sue me over a fifteen-year-old compressor, they can try. I just needed to know my reading wasn't crazy. Thanks for the talk.

The technician’s report you describe supports your reading of Section 14’s wear-and-tear exception. It does not establish that withholding payment is permitted under the full lease.

My recommendation remains: send a documented dispute rather than an unconditional refusal, and obtain a full-lease review before the payment deadline.
